And it has nothing to do with basketball or highway exits. That a man with zero horicultural training built one of the most internationally recognized private sculpture gardens in America out of plants rescued from a trash pile. and that the state contains a water tower shaped like an enormous anatomically detailed peach that has been causing traffic slowdowns on Interstate 85 since 1981. You start to wonder whether the whole state just collectively lost its mind at some point and nobody told you. I spent months tracking down the strangest corners of South Carolina and I found 12 towns that will genuinely make you question what normal even means. And South Carolina, trust me, has more than enough material. Let's count it down. Number 12, Hollywood. You come around a two-lane road, bend southwest of Charleston, and you see the sign Hollywood. It hits different when you're surrounded by marsh grass and Spanish moss instead of palm trees and film studios. Hollywood, South Carolina, sits in Charleston County, roughly 20 miles southwest of the city of Charleston, tucked between the Edisto River and the edge of the Ace Basin. The population hovers around 5,000 people, which means this Hollywood has fewer residents than a single building in the California version. The name, as best anyone can trace it, came from a local plantation that was named Hollywood in the early 1800s, long before California's version existed. The plantation name apparently referred to holly trees growing on the property, which is about as unglamorous an origin story as you could imagine. The name transferred to the surrounding community and stuck there, while the California town with the same name went on to become the center of the global entertainment industry. The South Carolina version remained a quiet agricultural and coastal community where shrimping boats matter more than film reels and nobody is trying to sell you a screenplay. What makes the detour worth it today is the combination of landscapes around the town, the Francis Marian National Forest to the north, the salt marshes stretching toward the coast, and the kind of rural quiet that the California Hollywood has not experienced in about a hundred years. Ask a local and they will tell you without a trace of irony that they prefer it. The land is quieter, the sky is bigger, and the only stars that matter here rise over the water. I cover towns like these every single week, and the next six entries are even weirder than what you've seen so far. Number 11, Due West. The first time you see due west on a map, you assume it's a placeholder, a directional marker accidentally printed as a town name by a cgrapher who forgot to go back and fill it in. But no, Due West is a real incorporated town in Abyville County in the Piedmont region of western South Carolina, sitting about 15 mi from Anderson. The population sits around 1,100 people, making it one of the smallest incorporated towns in the state, and yet it contains a 4-year college that has been continuously operating since 1839. The name has two competing origin stories, and historians have never fully settled which one is true. The first theory is straightforward. The settlement was located due west on a pioneer trail from another community and travelers simply started calling it that when giving directions. The name became informal shorthand that eventually became official. The second theory is more entertaining. It holds that the name is a corruption of Dwit's Corner, a colonial era settlement where American and Cherokee representatives signed a treaty in 1777. Over generations of spoken word geography, Dwit's corner slurred into due west through the kind of phonetic drift that gives linguists homework. What amplifies the strangeness considerably is Erskin College, which sits directly in the center of this tiny community. Erskin is a fully accredited liberal arts institution affiliated with the Associate Reformed Presbyterian Church, founded in 1839 and still enrolling students today. The college has a student body of roughly 600 people in a town of roughly 1,100. More than half of Due West's total population at any given moment is made up of students attending an institution that predates the Civil War. It is architecturally and demographically a university that has been accidentally placed inside someone else's small town. Both parties appear to have made their peace with the arrangement. Number 10, 45. When I first found this community on a state map, I genuinely assumed I had misread something. 45. Not the 45th precinct, not Highway 45, not the 45 acres development, just 45. A community in Greenwood County in the western part of South Carolina, roughly 15 miles northwest of the city of Greenwood. The population is in the low hundreds, and the community does not appear on most commercial maps unless you go looking for it specifically. The name, according to the oral histories that have been collected in the area over the years, most likely refers to the distance in miles from some notable point of origin, a colonial era road marker, a courthouse, or a survey reference used by early settlers when they were describing their location to outsiders. The number 45 became a landmark before the community had any other name, and the community took the number as its permanent identity when it needed one. What strikes visitors who make the trip is not the name itself. It's the absolute ordinariness of arriving in a community named like a math equation and finding it completely unremarkably normal. There's a church. There are houses and mailboxes and overgrown driveways. There is no irony in the air, no winking acknowledgement of the absurdity. Families have lived here for multiple generations under this numerically baffling name and found it as unexceptional as any other. The indifference is somehow the strangest part. It is a place that looked at every other town's naming conventions and decided a number was perfectly sufficient. The community has been right so far. Number nine, Sugar Tit. Yes, this is real. No, it is not on a novelty map someone printed for a bachelor party. Sugar Tit is a genuine community in Spartanberg County in the upstate region of South Carolina and it has appeared on official state and county maps for well over a century. The name, despite what it sounds like to 21st century ears, has a completely wholesome origin, or at least as wholesome as anything in the 19th century rural South could be. [music] In antibbellum southern households, the term sugar tit referred to a homemade infant pacifier. The device was typically made by knotting a cloth around a small lump of sugar or a piece of sweet food, then giving it to a fussy baby to suckle. It was a standard folk remedy, entirely unremarkable to the people using it. And when settlers gathered in this part of Spartanberg County, the name apparently attached itself to the community through one of those informal processes that nobody bothered to document, possibly from a nearby spring or watering spot known by that name among locals. The name was in common use before anyone thought to question whether posterity might find it awkward. The community made regional headlines in the early 2000s when a petition circulated to change the name citing professional embarrassment and the difficulty of explaining your mailing address to people outside the county. The petition did not succeed. Sugar tit remains sugar tit. A local moonshine brand subsequently adopted the name with something approaching maximum enthusiasm. The community itself is quiet, residential, and almost aggressively normal, which makes the sign at its edge feel like a punchline to a joke that the town itself never agreed to tell. Number eight, Pleion. Pilleon sits in Lexington County, about 20 m southwest of Colombia with a population of around 800 people. On any given Tuesday, it is one of the quieter communities in the Midlands of South Carolina. On the third Saturday of July each year, it transforms into something that makes [music] no sense for a town of 800 people. The Pelleon Peanut Party has been running for decades and draws attendance in the thousands with estimates sometimes pushing into the tens of thousands for the largest years to a community that does not have the infrastructure for that kind of crowd under ordinary circumstances. The festival is exactly what it sounds like, a celebration of the peanut farming heritage of the region. Featuring live music across multiple stages, carnival rides, fireworks, and more boiled peanuts than any reasonable person could consume. It is by almost every measure a wildly disproportionate event for the community hosting it. And the parking situation for surrounding roads becomes legendary in a bad way. Punctuating all of this is a large fiberglass peanut mounted on a pole at the edge of town. A roadside monument that stands as the permanent yearround ambassador of Pelleon's identity. The peanut pole has appeared in travel features, roadside attraction guides, and the personal photographs of thousands of people who pulled over specifically to be photographed next to a giant fiberglass legume on a stick. The town treats this object with complete sincerity. Pelion knows it has a peanut pole and it would like you to respect that. The annual party, the poll, and the conviction with which this community has committed to its peanut identity make Pelleon one of the most earnestly strange places in the state. Number seven, Ridgeway. Ridgeway is in Fairfield County, about 30 m north of Colombia on the old US Highway 21 corridor. With a population of approximately 300 people, it is by most measures one of the smallest incorporated towns in South Carolina and it has by self-declaration and by the evidence of any reasonable person's eyes, the world's smallest police station. The station is a repurposed structure roughly the dimensions of a large phone booth or a very small garden shed that sits on Ridgeway's main commercial block. The building has a telephone inside. It has the signage of an official police facility. It has at various points in its history been staffed by an actual police chief conducting actual police business. The Guinness World Records Connection has been claimed and displayed by the town over the years, though the official certification has shifted with competing claims from other jurisdictions. What has not shifted is the physical reality of the thing. This is a structure that a single adult can barely stand inside and it is the police station. The chief who served the station for decades became something of a local legend for taking the role with complete seriousness, conducting traffic stops, writing tickets, and generally policing a town of 300 people with the dedication of someone working in a much larger jurisdiction. The station has been photographed by road trippers, featured in statewide media, and referenced in travel guides for the better part of 40 years. Ridgeway is aware of what it has. It is not embarrassed. It has a sign pointing to the station from the main road. The sign is larger than the station it is pointing to. Number six, Johnston. Johnston is in Edgefield County, roughly 40 mi south of Aken along the South Carolina side of the Savannah River Valley with a population of about 2,300 people. It is the self-proclaimed peach capital of the world. That claim is made with complete sincerity stated on municipal signage without qualifiers and defended against all challengers. The challenger most frequently named is Georgia, specifically the Fort Valley area, which has made a competing claim to the same title and perhaps has better national name recognition for peaches. Here is what Johnston would like you to know. South Carolina is actually the second largest peach producing state in the United States by volume and has been for much of the last century. Georgia, despite its famous association with the fruit, ranks lower than South Carolina in actual production numbers, Johnston sits in the heart of that production region, surrounded by orchards that operate commercially in the summer. The claim, when you look at the agricultural statistics, is not as outrageous as it sounds. The peach festival that Johnston holds each summer draws people from across the region for peach ice cream, fresh peaches sold directly from orchards, peach flavored everything the vendors can think of, and the general atmosphere of a community that has decided its entire civic identity will be organized around a single fruit. The festival has run for decades. The town's water tower and official signage repeat the claim. And Johnston continues to look Georgia directly in the eye and say calmly and without raising its voice, "We have done the math and we are the capital. It is a very South Carolina thing to do." Number five, Gaffne. Gaffne is in Cherokee County in the northernmost part of South Carolina near the North Carolina border with a population of around 12,000 people. It sits along Interstate 85, which means millions of drivers pass through each year on their way between Charlotte and Atlanta. And very nearly all of them see what Gaffne has placed along the highway. The Peachoid is a water tower. It holds 1 million gallons of water. It stands 135 ft tall. It was constructed in 1981 at an original cost of around $5 million. And it was painted in careful and specific detail to look exactly like a peach down to the gradations of pink, red, and cream that give a real peach its characteristic blush and down to the vertical crease that gives a peach its distinctive silhouette. That silhouette at scale, viewed from a moving vehicle at highway speed, is startling in a way that has generated decades of jokes, comments, and near accidents. The structure was built to promote the Cherokee County peach industry and to celebrate the region's identity as a major peach producing area. The people who commissioned it understood what they were building. They built it anyway. The Peachoid became a genuine piece of American roadside culture, appearing in guide books, travel blogs, and eventually in the Netflix series House of Cards, where a character died in a distraction related traffic accident near it. The episode caused a documented spike in people making the drive to Gaffne specifically to see the tower. Gaffne took this in stride. The Peachoid is repainted on schedule. It holds its million gallons. It continues to cause double takes at 70 mph. It is first and foremost a functioning water tower. Everything else is secondary. It is named with a number and no amount of context fully softens the strangeness of seeing 96 on a road sign for the first time. The origin of the name is genuinely disputed which is itself unusual for a town that has existed since the colonial era. The most widely cited explanation is that the settlement was approximately 96 miles from the Cherokee village of Kioi, which was a major trading center in the colonial period, and that traders and settlers along the route began using the mileage as a landmark reference until it became the community's permanent name. A second theory involves a trader named Robert Guedi, who marked the distance on trade route records. A third, more romantic and less historically documented, involves a Native American woman warning a British soldier with the number 96 appearing somewhere in the transmission of that warning. What nobody disputes is what happened here. The Battle of 96 fought in November 1775 was the first land battle of the American Revolution in the South, months before the Declaration of Independence was signed. The siege of 96 in 1781 was one of the longest sustained sieges of the entire Revolutionary War. The earthworks of the Star Fort, which colonial era soldiers built and then fought over, are still visible and preserved today as part of the 96 National Historic Site, a National Park Service unit that receives visitors from around the country. You can walk the same ground where soldiers fought and died. The town that contains this history is named with a number. The number is 96. The juxtaposition is unsettling in exactly the right way. Number three, Bishopville. Bishopville is the county seat of Lee County in the central part of South Carolina, roughly 45 mi southeast of Colombia with a population around 3,200 people. It is the kind of quiet, flat Midlands town that appears from the outside [music] to have no particular claim on anyone's attention. Then you actually go there. Pearl Frier was a black man who grew up in a family of sharecroers and moved to Bishopville in the early 1980s. He had no horicultural training. He had no art background. He wanted to win a yard of the month award in his new neighborhood. And there are accounts, including his own, that suggest local nurseries were unwilling to sell him the plants he needed. With racial bias playing a role in that resistance, he began collecting discarded plants from a nursery's discard pile. Instead, he began teaching himself topiary, the art of pruning and sculpting living plants into deliberate shapes through experimentation on plants that were otherwise headed for the compost. Over the course of decades, Frier transformed three acres of his property into a landscape that has been called, without exaggeration, one of the most extraordinary private gardens in the United States. Thousands of plants shaped into spirals, arches, and abstract forms that reach 20 and 30 feet into the air. The Smithsonian magazine called him the Picasso of plants. His work was exhibited at international venues, a documentary about his life screened at festivals across the country. He passed away in 2024, but the garden remains open to visitors and continues to be maintained by the foundation that now stewards it. A few miles from the garden is the Button King Museum. Dalton Stevens, a Bishopville resident who gave himself the title Button King, began his project during an extended bout of insomnia in the 1980s. He started sewing buttons onto a pair of jeans one night because he needed something to do with his hands. He could not stop. By the time he finished, he had covered an entire suit, multiple vehicles, including a car and a hearse, household furniture, a coffin, and the exterior walls of his home, over 600,000 individual buttons, all sewn by hand across objects that are now displayed in the museum with the seriousness of a gallery installation. Bishopville did not plan to become a destination. It became one anyway. Number two, Mars Bluff. Mars Bluff is an unincorporated community in Florence County in the PD region of eastern South Carolina, roughly 10 mi east of Florence itself. The name sounds like it belongs in a science fiction serial from the 1950s. The event that defined this community's place in history happened in 1958, which is close enough. On March 11th, 1958, a United States Air Force B47 Stratet bomber was flying over South Carolina as part of a routine transport mission carrying a nuclear weapon from Hunter Air Force Base in Savannah, Georgia to its destination. A crew member entered the bomb bay to perform a check and accidentally triggered the emergency release mechanism. The bomb, a Mark 6 nuclear device roughly 12 feet long and weighing nearly 7,600 lb, fell from the aircraft over the PD region of South Carolina. The reason this is not the most catastrophic peaceime accident in American history is a matter of inventory. The nuclear capsule, the fistal uranium, and plutonium core required for an actual nuclear detonation had not been inserted into the weapon prior to the flight. What the bomb did contain was its conventional explosive trigger, which amounted to thousands of pounds of TNT. When the bomb struck the yard of a local man named Walter Greg, that trigger detonated. The explosion destroyed the Greg family's home. It injured six members of the family, including children. It left a crater approximately 70 ft wide and 35 ft deep. Trees were stripped for hundreds of yards around the impact point. The federal government paid the Greg family $54,000 in damages, a settlement that adjusted for inflation amounts to roughly half a million dollars today. A historical marker was placed near the site in later years. The crater partially filled in over the decades is still visible on the property. Mars Bluff is a community that has had a nuclear bomb detonate in it, has a name that sounds like a NASA mission designation, and has a historical marker where a family's house used to stand.
